analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for businesses to classify workers as independent contractors for federal employment taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into law fixed standards for deciding whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor for federal employment taxes. It gives businesses a set of "safe harbors" — conditions under which they can treat a worker as a contractor without fear the IRS will later demand back payroll taxes. It also bars the Treasury Department from issuing new regulations or rulings on employment status, and it shifts the burden of proof to the IRS in classification disputes. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that rely on contractor labor gain the most: they get clear, written standards they can rely on, protection from retroactive payroll-tax assessments going back decades, and a lighter burden of proof in IRS disputes. Genuine independent contractors also gain a clear rule for their status. The bill repeals the older Section 530 safe harbor but replaces it with similar statutory standards.

how_it_helps.text: A business that files returns consistent with treating a worker as a contractor is "deemed" correct unless the IRS shows it had no reasonable basis for that treatment, protecting it from retroactive employment-tax assessments for periods back to 1978 [S2][S3].

The bill creates statutory safe harbors: if a worker bears significant cost for equipment, is paid based on output or rates rather than hours, and substantially controls how the work is done, the worker is not an employee for tax purposes [S2][S3].
Once a business makes a prima facie case that its classification was reasonable and cooperates with the IRS, the burden of proof shifts to the Treasury Secretary [S3].

Genuine independent contractors gain certainty: a written contract meeting the safe harbor means the worker is definitively not an employee for federal tax purposes, ending classification disputes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays through lost employment-tax revenue where workers who function as employees are reclassified as contractors. Those workers also bear a cost: Social Security and Medicare payroll-tax coverage and the employer-side benefits that come with employee status depend on that classification.

drawbacks.text: By making contractor classification easier and safer for businesses, the bill increases the incentive to classify workers as contractors who function like employees — leaving them without employer-side Social Security and Medicare contributions and with a larger self-employment tax load [S3].

The bill prohibits Treasury and the IRS from publishing any new regulations or revenue rulings on employment status for employment-tax purposes, limiting the government's ability to adapt guidance to new work arrangements [S3].
The safe harbor excludes engineers, designers, drafters, computer programmers, systems analysts, and similar skilled workers, so the protection is carved out unevenly across occupations [S3].

The bill repeals Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978, the long-standing safe harbor businesses have relied on since 1978, which could unsettle existing classifications until the new standards take effect the following year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real case for the bill: classification rules were genuinely vague, and both honest businesses and genuine contractors bore the cost of unpredictable IRS disputes. But the bill's protection is one-sided. It shields the business from back payroll taxes while doing nothing to secure Social Security, Medicare, or benefit coverage for workers who are reclassified out of employee status, and it forbids the agency from issuing new guidance. On balance it is a tax-administration bill written largely around the employer's side of the table.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing or vote there, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Erik Paulsen introduced the bill on May 20, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
Six other House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractor-heavy businesses are no worse off: they keep the status quo, including the Section 530 safe harbor the bill would have replaced. Workers avoided the bill's loosened path to contractor classification, and the Treasury kept current employment-tax enforcement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses kept the status quo; no one lost ground

industries.industry: Businesses that use contractor and staffing labor
industries.note: The bill gives these employers a statutory safe harbor to classify workers as independent contractors and shields them from retroactive payroll-tax assessments. The gain comes from avoiding employment taxes and the cost of employee classification, a cost that otherwise funds workers' Social Security and Medicare.
Genuine contractors get a clear written standard confirming their status and ending unpredictable IRS classification disputes.
The bill cuts off retroactive assessments and bars the agencies from issuing new guidance on employment status, shrinking both revenue and regulatory flexibility.
